disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the diabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is 6.5% or above, the range used to diagnose diabetes. A single result is not a diagnosis: your doctor will confirm it with a repeat test or another blood test.

summary: Your HbA1c of 6.5 is in the diabetes range, which means your blood sugar levels have been higher than ideal for some time. Along with your weight being above the healthy range and a family history of diabetes, these factors suggest it's a good time to focus on your health. The most valuable next steps are following up with blood sugar monitoring tests like fasting glucose and post-meal readings, staying active regularly, and working toward your calorie target of 1850 calories a day to support a healthy weight.

foods_to_eat: Brown rice and whole grains instead of white rice
Leafy greens like bok choy, spinach, and choy sum
Tofu, edamame, and other soy foods
Fatty fish like mackerel and salmon
Nuts and seeds in small amounts
foods_to_avoid: Sugary drinks like bubble tea and sweetened sodas
White rice in large portions and refined noodles
Deep-fried items like tempura and fried dumplings
Sweet sauces high in sugar, such as sweet chili or teriyaki glaze
Processed meats like sausages and fried spam
Sweetened condensed milk and sweet desserts
plan.portion_guidance: Fill about half your bowl or plate with vegetables, a quarter with whole grains like brown rice, and a quarter with a protein source like fish, tofu, or lean meat. Use a small bowl for rice rather than a large one to keep portions moderate.
plan.hydration: Aim for about 8 to 10 cups of water through the day. Unsweetened green tea is a good addition. Limit sugary drinks and juices.
based_on: HbA1c in the diabetes range: low-glycaemic, high-fibre focus

exercise: Since you're already moderately active, build toward at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, like brisk walking, cycling, or swimming, spread across most days.
Add muscle-strengthening activities on 2 days a week, such as bodyweight exercises, resistance bands, or light weights, with a day of rest between sessions.
Increase intensity or duration gradually, by about 10 percent a week, to avoid injury.
lifestyle.walking_goal: Start with 20-25 minutes of brisk walking 5 days a week, and build up over a few weeks to 30 minutes a day, 5-6 days a week.
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI falls in the overweight category, so gradually working toward a modestly lower body weight can help improve how your body manages blood sugar. Focus on steady, sustainable changes rather than quick fixes, such as portion awareness, more vegetables and fiber, and regular activity.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night. Keep a consistent sleep and wake time, limit screens for an hour before bed, and keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet to support better rest.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for 5 minutes daily, especially during busy or tense moments.
Try a short daily mindfulness or meditation practice using a free app or guided audio.
Consider regular physical activity and time outdoors, both of which help lower stress naturally.
behaviour_change: Since your HbA1c is in the diabetes range, regular self-monitoring and follow-up with a healthcare provider can help you track progress over time.
Build small, consistent habits, like a daily walk or a vegetable with every meal, rather than trying to change everything at once.
Keep a simple log of your meals, activity, and sleep for a few weeks to spot patterns and opportunities for improvement.

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Shows your average blood glucose over about 3 months and whether your plan is working.
monitoring.frequency: Every 3 months until your doctor says you are at target, then every 6 months

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Post-meal (post-prandial) blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows how your body handles glucose after meals, which HbA1c alone can hide.

monitoring.name: Lipid profile (cholesterol)
monitoring.why: Diabetes and high cholesterol together raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
monitoring.frequency: Every year (at least every 5 years if you are under 40), or as your doctor advises
risk_indicators: Existing cholesterol problem or heart disease

monitoring.name: Kidney function (eGFR) and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
monitoring.why: High glucose and blood pressure can quietly damage the kidneys; these tests find it early.
monitoring.frequency: Every year, or more often if you already have kidney disease

monitoring.name: Vitamin B12
monitoring.why: Metformin, a common diabetes medicine, can lower B12 over time; low B12 can mimic nerve damage.
monitoring.frequency: Ask your doctor, especially if you take metformin (often checked yearly)
risk_indicators: Vegetarian or vegan diet (lower dietary B12)

monitoring.name: Dilated eye examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can damage the retina (diabetic retinopathy) long before your vision changes.
monitoring.frequency: Soon after diabetes is confirmed, then every year (your eye doctor may extend this to every 2 years if exams stay clear)

monitoring.name: Foot examination
monitoring.why: Diabetes can reduce feeling and blood flow in the feet, so small injuries go unnoticed.
monitoring.frequency: A full exam every year; check your own feet daily

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

monitoring.name: Cardiovascular risk assessment
monitoring.why: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in people with diabetes.

preventive_actions: Aim for regular physical activity most days of the week, such as brisk walking or similar moderate exercise.
Work toward your daily calorie target of 1850 calories through balanced, portion-controlled meals.
Schedule routine monitoring tests such as fasting blood sugar, post-meal blood sugar, and lipid profile as recommended.
Keep track of your blood pressure regularly since it often relates to blood sugar and weight management.
Prioritize a dilated eye exam and foot examination at recommended intervals to catch early changes.
Build habits that support gradual, sustainable weight loss given your overweight BMI category.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
